title: The Galaxy Brains of YT Fitness have ruined science
summary: First part of a trilogy attacking the 'meme science' of YouTube fitness: dogmatic, zealous, smug, self-obsessed, unbending and used to shut down debate and sell products. He argues studies on movement, stimulus and diet are misused, that personal experience and self-programming are the real science, and calls himself anti-science in that sense.
claims: He distinguishes the rigorous scientific process, which he respects, from the 'meme science' used on YouTube fitness, which skips steps and is therefore fraudulent
He deliberately never cites or links studies or uses them as arguments of authority; his channel is built on his own experience of what worked for him
Being 'anti-science' for him means being against what science has become on YouTube, not against the actual practice of science
Real science is anti-dogma, but science channels present one paper as the truth, then silently switch to the next paper without ever admitting they pushed wrong ideas for years
He gives information as his opinion precisely so that if it changes he can simply say it changed, rather than having staked his identity on a study
Followers of YouTube science behave like a religious cult: they believe whatever the scientific community says and label dissenters 'anti-science' like heretics
A scientific finding is true only on a timeline; treating a paper as fixed final truth turns science into ideology
Papers must be interpreted and are not free of subjectivity; the same stats can be made to say many different things
Linking a paper in a comment argument to end the discussion is anti-speech and stops people from thinking together
He predicts science-based fitness channels will gradually lose traction and gain detractors as people tire of them
YouTube fitness evolved from big uneducated bros, to relatable everyday guys, to science-branded channels that everyone copied for views
YouTube fitness is powerlifting-centric and, beyond that, science-centric; 'scientific' has become a marketing label
Science is the perfect sales tool: it sells the promise of results and, when the product fails, lets the seller blame the buyer's genetics
Using the title 'Doctor' on fitness channels is a built-in argument of authority, often for PhDs unrelated to training
Universal visual movement cues do not work because bone lengths, hip sockets and back responses differ; only broad things to avoid for engagement and injury prevention are universal
For movement you only need to understand leverages, center of gravity of the weight and body, and angles (back, shoulder, elbow, foot angles)
Studies comparing exercise variations on a spectrum often wrongly conclude two lifts are equivalent, e.g. trap bar deadlift versus conventional deadlift
People arguing with studies have usually only read the abstract, found via search engines that feed confirmation bias; you can always find a study to support any theory
He has met one-heavy-set trainees and people doing 10x10 at about 45% intensity year-round who could each produce studies proving they were right
He quotes Rabelais: science without conscience is the ruin of the soul, meaning both morals and understanding
Researchers chase spicy, clickable findings such as leg press beating squats or flyes beating bench for chest activation; better stretch or activation does not mean more growth
When he actually reads and dismantles a study someone throws at him, the response is always silence because they only wanted to win
Optimal stimulus depends on the individual's level; 'more volume is always better' may only hold for the speaker, so programming must be experimented with case by case
Coaches publish programming studies to convince you they know better so you pay them for a program
Diet science is the worst area: people identify emotionally with their diet (vegans and carnivores alike) and many nutrition studies are industry-funded with deliberately chosen subjects
He avoids making many diet videos because he thinks logic has deserted that topic and it is now pure emotion
Science and personal experience should work together: studies give broad group generalizations, but they are worthless until you test them on yourself
Your opinion and critical thinking when reading a study matter as much as the study itself
Programming is the one science natural bodybuilders truly need; you are the subject, director and peer reviewer of your own experiment
Someone who trains 10 years, takes notes, learns to program and eats well is more of a scientist than paper-waving YouTubers
People who rely heavily on science tend to be small: lacking physicality, they argue with papers against people far stronger than them
He learned everything from YouTube fitness plus his own action and reflection; never read a book on programming or a study on curls
He says he will never make money from the channel; his one goal is helping natural bodybuilders reach their potential
